alt: Eight small family diagrams: nuclear (two parents and children), horizontal extended (two couples of the same generation with their children), beanpole (four generations with few members each), modified extended (relatives in separate homes keeping contact), reconstituted (a step-family), lone parent, empty nest (children have left) and childless.
caption: Family structures differ in how many generations and how many members per generation they hold.

after: ## How are demographic changes affecting families? (4.3.1)
alt: Two family trees. A wide, short family has many children and fewer generations alive; a long, thin beanpole family has four generations with few members each. Below, three causes: falling birth rates make families smaller, longer life expectancy adds generations, and parenthood comes later.
caption: Fewer births and longer lives turn wide families into tall, thin beanpoles.

alt: The New Right argue the married two-parent nuclear family is best and link non-traditional families to poor socialisation. Postmodernists such as Judith Stacey see diversity as positive. Robert Chester adds that most people still spend part of their lives in a nuclear family, often a neo-conventional one.
caption: The New Right fear diversity, postmodernists welcome it, and Chester says the nuclear family is still common.

after: ## Did industrialisation create the nuclear family? (4.3.2)
alt: Parsons claimed the mobile nuclear family fits industrial society. On a timeline, Laslett (1972) found nuclear households were already common in pre-industrial England, and Anderson (1971) found working-class families in 1851 Preston sharing homes with relatives to cope with industrial hardship.
caption: Historians found nuclear families before industry and extended living during it.

after: ## Why are marriage, divorce and cohabitation changing? (4.3.3 and 4.3.4)
alt: Factors loosening the pressure to marry or stay married: easier divorce laws, less stigma, secularisation, female empowerment and the internet widening partner choice. Cultural expectations of early, arranged marriage hold traditions in place. Alternatives to marriage include cohabitation, singlehood, lone parenthood and civil partnerships.
caption: Most forces loosen marriage; cultural expectations can still hold it in place.

alt: Three changes in roles: partners moving from segregated to more joint roles, though feminists find women still do most domestic work; children changing from an economic asset to a cost; grandparents giving childcare and support but sometimes needing care. The sandwich generation cares for both elderly parents and children.
caption: Roles are shifting for partners, children and grandparents, and the middle generation is squeezed.
